content:
Quick answer: There is no single best supplement for everyone with joint pain. Evidence depends on the product and type of arthritis, and supplements can interact with medicines. NICE says not to offer glucosamine for osteoarthritis. Ask your pharmacist or treating clinician before starting a product, and do not replace prescribed treatment.

Start with the cause of joint pain

Joint pain has different causes. A supplement study in rheumatoid arthritis does not establish a benefit for osteoarthritis or unexplained pain. Discuss persistent or changing symptoms with your GP rather than relying on a product label.

What current guidance can and cannot tell you
ProductEvidence and limitsPractical check
GlucosamineNICE says not to offer it to manage osteoarthritis because there is no strong evidence of benefit.Do not take an online product ranking as a reason to start it. Ask a pharmacist about any product you already use.
Turmeric or curcuminNCCIH describes initial osteoarthritis evidence as positive but not definitive. Products and absorption-enhancing ingredients differ.Some enhanced-absorption products have been linked to liver damage. Check the exact product and medicines first.
GingerMay help knee osteoarthritis symptoms, but much of the research has been poor quality.Digestive side effects and medicine interactions matter; food and extracts are different.
Omega-3Some rheumatoid-arthritis evidence suggests possible symptom benefit as an addition to drug treatment; this does not prove a benefit for all joint pain.Do not alter prescribed rheumatoid-arthritis medicines on this basis. Discuss supplements with your team.
Vitamin DImportant for bones and muscles. General UK vitamin-D advice is not proof that higher doses treat arthritis pain.NHS advises considering 10 micrograms daily in autumn and winter for adults; some groups need it all year. Deficiency treatment is an individual clinical decision.

Do not stack products or copy trial doses

More is not necessarily better. Products may share ingredients, and a research dose may not suit your medicines or health conditions. This guide does not recommend a therapeutic dose, a brand or a supplement trial period.

What should I tell my pharmacist?

  • The exact product name, ingredients and amount per dose.
  • All prescribed and non-prescription medicines and other supplements.
  • Any health conditions, pregnancy or breastfeeding.
  • What symptom you hope to change and any side effects you have noticed.

NHS SPS advises that no interaction information does not mean no interaction is possible. Do not stop conventional medicines without consulting your healthcare professional. Keep complementary products on your medicine list.

Warning signs

Report new or worsening symptoms to a healthcare professional. If you take turmeric or curcumin and develop dark urine or yellow skin or eyes, stop the product and seek medical advice promptly. For a severe or life-threatening reaction, call 999.

Where to go next

Read our medicine and supplement interaction guide, ginger and turmeric comparison and arthritis diet guide. Use them to prepare questions, not to replace personal advice.
